title: 2. Units: what "compute" actually means
heading: Units: what compute actually means
label: Units
summary: Why compute is not one substance, and how power, energy, stock and flow differ.

blocks.text: 2.1 Compute is not one physical substance

spans.text: "Compute" is a bundle of resources used to execute numerical operations. In modern AI, that bundle includes accelerator chips, high-bandwidth memory, interconnects, host CPUs, storage, networking, power conversion, cooling, buildings, software, and people. A cluster can have many theoretical FLOPs but deliver poor useful performance if memory bandwidth, networking, reliability, or software is weak.

A watt is a rate of using energy. A watt-hour is an amount of energy. Industry discussion uses megawatts and gigawatts as a shorthand for cluster scale.

blocks.text: 2.3 Why watts are used as a proxy

spans.text: Chips require electricity, so power availability puts a hard upper bound on the cluster. It is often easier to estimate contracted megawatts than secret chip counts. Yet equal watts do not imply equal compute:

items.text: a newer accelerator may provide more operations per watt;
lower precision can increase peak arithmetic throughput;
better networking and software can raise utilization;
one workload may be memory-bound while another is compute-bound;
a cluster may sit idle or be unavailable due to failures;
a Chinese domestic accelerator and a frontier Western accelerator may deliver different useful work per watt.

If new machines are much more efficient than old machines, the newest year's additions can be a modest fraction of electrical capacity but a large fraction of useful FLOPs. The centralization argument (
) relies on this composition effect: capture a large share of new capacity while each new watt is more productive than the legacy stock.
